title: A huge earthquake seems to have woken a volcano that had been quiet for centuries
body: On 30 July 2025 a magnitude 8.8 earthquake struck in the ocean off Russia’s Kamchatka Peninsula. A few days later Krasheninnikov, a pair of volcanoes on the peninsula’s Pacific coast, began erupting for the first time in nearly five centuries, apparently jolted awake by the quake. Kamchatka’s busiest volcanoes are watched with instruments on the ground, but quiet Krasheninnikov was not; instead the NASA–ISRO radar satellite **NISAR**, which images the same spot twice every 12 days, caught it. From 17 of its radar images, researchers built a time-lapse of the lava filling an inner caldera, spilling into a wider crater and spreading east as a fan.

cover.alt: Radar image in orange tones of a volcano with two craters, light streaks of lava fanning down one side
cover.credit: NASA Scientific Visualization Studio · Public domain

slides.alt: Animation that zooms from a globe of the north-west Pacific down to the Kamchatka Peninsula and a volcano, then shows a sequence of orange-tinted radar images in 3D: light-coloured lava fills a small crater, overflows it and spreads downhill in a widening fan of streaks.
slides.caption: Zooming in on Kamchatka, then images of Krasheninnikov from the radar satellite NISAR, 25 December 2025 to 17 August 2026: lava shows up lighter as it fills the crater and fans out downhill.
slides.credit: NASA Scientific Visualization Studio · Public domain · excerpt

slides.heading: A very long nap
slides.note: NASA dates its last eruption to about 1550; some sources say a century earlier

events.text: A few days later, Krasheninnikov starts erupting
NISAR takes its first image of the eruption
The latest frame: the lava fan is still spreading

slides.prompt: Each pixel in NISAR’s images of the volcano covers how much ground?
slides.detail: Roughly half a tennis court. Lava reflects the radar’s microwaves more brightly than the snow or bare ground around it, so it shows up lighter.

slides.question: Why was Krasheninnikov not closely watched by instruments on the ground?
options: It had been quiet for centuries
slides.explanation: Kamchatka’s frequently erupting volcanoes are closely monitored from the ground. Krasheninnikov, quiet for centuries, was not, so the satellite’s radar view was all the more valuable.

source.label: NASA SVS: US-India Satellite Captures Time-Lapse Video of Volcanic Eruption
